analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal right to full promised pay, paystubs, timely final paychecks, and triple damages for wage theft.
analysis.headline: The bill won 32 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, but never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened federal wage-and-hour law for workers whose employers don't pay them what they earned. It created a federal right to be paid the wage rate promised in any contract, required pay disclosure at hire and itemized paystubs, required final paychecks within 14 days of leaving a job, and let workers recover unpaid wages plus interest and double or triple damages. It also raised fines on violating employers to as much as $110,150 per employee, blocked employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims, and funded $50 million a year in grants for community groups that help workers recover stolen wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially low-wage workers in restaurants, retail, home care, and other industries with high rates of wage theft, who the bill's findings say lose an estimated $15 billion a year to unpaid wages. The bill would give them the pay rate promised in their contract, itemized paystubs, final paychecks within 14 days of leaving a job, the right to see their employer's payroll records within 21 days, and a 4-to-5-year window to sue instead of 2-to-3. Workers could recover unpaid wages plus interest and liquidated damages equal to double or triple the loss, and could not be forced to sign away their right to a group court claim as a condition of employment. Worker advocacy groups, legal aid organizations, and unions would gain access to new federal grant funding to educate workers and help them file claims.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to full compensation: if an employment contract or union agreement promises a pay rate above the federal minimum, the employer must pay it (the bill repeals existing law allowing employers to pay only the minimum regardless of contract).

Requires employers to disclose pay rates and exemption classifications at hire, provide itemized paystubs showing hours, rates, overtime, and deductions, and deliver all final pay and benefits within 14 days of termination, with daily pay owed for each day the final payment is late.

Raises the stakes for violations: workers recover unpaid wages plus interest and liquidated damages equal to 2 times the loss (3 times for retaliation cases), and employers face civil fines up to $22,030 per employee per violation, or up to $110,150 for repeated or willful violations.

Extends the time workers have to sue from 2 years (3 for willful violations) to 4 years (5 for willful), suspends that clock while the Labor Department investigates, and gives employees a right to copies of their payroll records within 21 days, with the worker's own testimony presumed accurate if the employer kept no proper records.
Bars employers from forcing workers to waive, through arbitration agreements, the right to bring wage claims in court individually or as a class or collective action.

Requires the Labor Department to refer willful offenders who falsify payroll records to the Justice Department for prosecution, and authorizes $50 million a year from fiscal 2024 through 2027 in grants to nonprofits, unions, and other community partners to educate workers and help them recover unpaid wages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who fail to pay workers what they earned would owe back pay plus interest, liquidated damages of up to three times the wages withheld, and civil fines up to $110,150 per employee for repeated or willful violations. All covered employers would bear new administrative costs for hire-date pay disclosures, itemized paystubs, 14-day final paychecks, and 21-day turnaround on payroll record requests. Grant funding, up to $50 million a year, would come from the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that withhold or underpay wages

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on all covered employers, not just violators: businesses would need new systems for hire-date pay disclosures, expanded itemized paystubs, 14-day final payments, and 21-day responses to employee record requests, a heavier lift for small firms than for large ones.

Higher damages (double or triple the unpaid wages plus interest) and a presumption in the worker's favor when records are missing would increase litigation exposure, which critics of such measures argue leads to more lawsuits and settlement pressure on employers even in borderline cases.

The bill directs $50 million a year in taxpayer-funded grants to nonprofits, unions, and advocacy groups to assist enforcement, which opponents would describe as public funding for advocacy organizations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall mostly on employers who are already breaking the law, since the fines and multiplied damages attach only to violations, and the bill's findings note that one-third of employers caught stealing wages kept doing so because penalties were too light. The genuine costs are the new paperwork burdens on all employers, especially small ones, and the risk of more wage litigation. For workers who lose an estimated $15 billion a year to unpaid wages, the protections are large; the compliance burden on honest businesses is real but comparatively modest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, so it never got a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on September 12, 2023 with 30 original cosponsors, all of them Democrats plus independent Bernie Sanders, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the full cosponsor list settled at 32, all Senate Democrats and independents.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died under Senate Rule XL, which requires bills to be reintroduced to be considered again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay their workers are better off, because they continue to face only the old 2-to-3-year lawsuit window, an equal-amounts liquidated damages rule, light civil fines, and no federal paystub or final-paycheck mandate.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee; she was the lead sponsor

for.name: 31 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up nearly two-thirds of the Democratic caucus

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders (as HELP Chairman)
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to no hearing or markup; no committee action was ever taken on the bill after referral

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in two years; it appears only as a referral in the action record

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill; under the Senate's practice of needing 60 votes to advance most bills, its lack of any Republican support left it without a path even if scheduled

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; because no vote was ever held, the partisan split shows up in sponsorship rather than a roll call.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, fast food, retail, janitorial, home care)
industries.note: These industries have the highest rates of minimum wage and overtime violations, and the bill would require them to pay back wages with interest, double or triple damages, and fines up to $110,150 per employee for repeat violations. The bill's findings note compliance with wage law runs below 50 percent in some of these industries.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies, subcontractors, and gig businesses relying on worker misclassification
industries.note: The bill's required disclosures would force employers to state on hire whether they are classifying a worker as exempt from minimum wage or overtime protections, and the extended 4-to-5-year lawsuit window and record-presumption rule make misclassification claims easier and cheaper to bring.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy nonprofits
industries.note: The bill defines them as eligible grant recipients under a new $50 million-a-year program to educate workers and help them file and prove wage claims.
The bill's findings argue that wage theft puts compliant employers at a competitive disadvantage against violators; stronger penalties narrow that gap.
